examples.knowledge_point: Evaluating Infinite Limits Using the Laws of Exponents and the Algebra of Limits
examples.worked_solution:
We can use the laws of exponents and the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }-5{(\frac{1}{3})}^{1+x} & =-5{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{3})}^{1+x} \\  & =-5{lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{3})}^{1}\cdot {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x} \\  & =-5{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{3}\cdot {(\frac{1}{3})}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}\cdot {lim}_{x\to \infty }{(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the graph of $y = \left(\dfrac 1 3\right)^x.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13943873/assets/81be7f2983aeb647a8fa88e2caad8cea3c2052190222670838077e760a2e7fda.png)

From the graph, we see that the function decreases to zero as $x$ increases. So

$$
\lim_\limits{x \to \infty}   \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x} = 0,
$$

and finally, we have

$$
-\dfrac{5}{3}\cdot \lim_\limits{x \to \infty}   \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x} = -\dfrac 5 3\cdot 0 = 0.
$$
